name: Red light glasses

lead: Red light glasses are strongly tinted lenses worn in the evening, usually at home with screens or indoor lighting, to cut the blue and short-wavelength light that can suppress melatonin. People wear them hoping for easier sleep, since better sleep is tied to skin, eyes and energy in appearance discussions.

The broader category of blue-light filtering glasses has been studied for sleep, and a 2009 randomized trial and later systematic reviews of evening blue-blocking glasses exist, with mixed results reported by different professional bodies.

paras: They are put on a few hours before bed and worn while using screens or indoor lights, often alongside dimming lights and a regular sleep schedule. Wearers typically judge results by how quickly they fall asleep and how they look and feel the next day.

The lenses are generally considered low-risk. The American Academy of Ophthalmology does not recommend special eyewear for computer use, and the UK College of Optometrists states the best available evidence does not support blue-blocking lenses to improve sleep in the general population.

More rested look: fresher skin and eyes
angle.text: People wear them in the evening to support sleep, which they connect to how rested the face and skin look the next day. The link from glasses to sleep is what proponents claim and what researchers have examined with mixed findings.

lead: Red light glasses are tinted glasses, in red or amber shades, worn at night to block blue and green wavelengths from screens and lighting. The idea is that evening light, particularly short-wavelength light, signals the body clock to stay alert, so filtering it may help sleep come easier.

In appearance-focused communities, sleep is treated as a foundation: rested people are described as looking fresher, with fewer dark circles and better skin. Red light glasses are a low-effort way people use to try to improve that sleep.

Blue-light filtering glasses became popular by the end of the 2010s and are marketed for problems from eye strain to sleep disruption [1]. Organisations differ in their conclusions: the American Academy of Ophthalmology does not recommend special eyewear for computer use, and the UK College of Optometrists says the best available evidence does not support blue-blocking lenses for sleep quality in the general population [1]. Clinical research on evening amber lenses includes a 2009 randomized trial and systematic reviews for sleep and mood disorders [2].

paras: Blue-light filtering glasses range from slightly yellow tints to heavy amber or red lenses [1]. The more strongly tinted versions are the ones people describe as red light or amber glasses, worn mainly after dark.

Published research includes a 2009 randomized trial of amber lenses to block blue light and improve sleep [2], a 2021 systematic review of evening blue-blocking glasses for sleep and mood disorders [2], and studies in athletes testing evening short-wavelength light restriction [2]. Reviews of the wider blue-light glasses category report that several studies found blue light from computers does not cause eye disease, and that eye strain relates more to prolonged use [1].

The American Academy of Ophthalmology does not recommend special eyewear for computer use, and the UK College of Optometrists states that the best available evidence does not support blue-blocking lenses for sleep in the general population [1]. Reducing evening screen time and using night mode are noted as alternatives [1].
